clusters.name: Standard protections — the safe norm
clusters.theme: The buyer cannot walk away from the deal over broad outside problems — economic downturns, industry-wide slumps, wars, pandemics, or changes in law — unless the target company is hit noticeably harder than its competitors. This is today's market-standard wording, and 22 of the 30 deals use it.
clusters.representative_clause_excerpt: Material Adverse Effect shall not include any effect resulting from (a) general economic or political conditions, (b) conditions generally affecting Target's industries, (c) acts of war, terrorism, pandemics, or natural disasters, (d) changes in Law or GAAP; provided that (a)-(d) apply only to the extent the effect disproportionately affects Target relative to industry peers.
clusters.why_distinct: Modern default template — four standard carve-out buckets present, all gated by the disproportionate-impact hook applied uniformly. Contemporary M&A practice has converged on this shape; deviations signal idiosyncratic negotiation.

clusters.name: Pandemic risk shifted to one side
clusters.theme: Almost the standard wording, but the pandemic exception is rewritten so that COVID-style losses land specifically on the buyer — a deliberate reallocation of risk that a reviewer should flag.
clusters.representative_clause_excerpt: Notwithstanding the foregoing carve-outs (economic, industry-wide, war/terrorism, changes in Law), the parties EXPLICITLY allocate to BUYER any effect of the COVID-19 pandemic on the Company's business — no disproportionate-impact hook applies to pandemic effects; pandemic risk is contractually buyer's burden.
clusters.why_distinct: Both deals depart from Cluster 1 by treating the pandemic clause asymmetrically — Pfizer/Seagen by removing the disproportionate-impact hook from pandemic effects only, Forescout/Advent by contractually allocating COVID-19 risk to the buyer. The structural feature in common is that pandemic risk is NOT pooled with the other carve-outs.

clusters.name: Judgment-based, not a checklist
clusters.theme: No fixed list of exceptions at all. Whether the buyer can exit instead hinges on a forward-looking judgment about lasting damage to the company's long-term earning power — short-term blips don't count.
clusters.representative_clause_excerpt: Material Adverse Effect means any effect that has had or would reasonably be expected to have a durationally-significant material adverse effect on the long-term earnings power of the Company. The forward-looking 'reasonably be expected to' standard governs; short-term variations do not qualify.
clusters.why_distinct: These deals do not negotiate carve-outs at all — they govern via the IBP/Tyson durationally-significant forward-looking standard. Industry-wide comparison is implicit in the long-term-earnings-power lens, not enumerated. This is the foundational Strine template and predates the modern carve-out norm.

clusters.name: A separate back-door exit
clusters.theme: The standard exceptions are present, but a separate "keep running the business as usual" promise can independently let the buyer walk away — even when the main walk-away clause would have protected the seller. This is the gap that unwound the Tiffany / LVMH and AB Stable deals.
clusters.representative_clause_excerpt: MAE excludes economic, industry-wide, war/terrorism, and law/GAAP effects subject to the disproportionate-impact hook. The Ordinary Course covenant in Section 5.1 operates INDEPENDENTLY of these MAE carve-outs — pandemic effects can clear the MAE bar and still breach Ordinary Course.
clusters.why_distinct: Both contracts pair a standard MAE carve-out list with an explicit gap between MAE risk allocation and the Ordinary Course covenant — the AB Stable / MAPS reading. A buyer cannot rely on a clean MAE result to discharge an Ordinary Course breach. The structural feature in common is the SEPARATION of the two closing-condition rails.

outliers.why: The dangerous one. Its walk-away clause is missing almost every standard protection — no exception for industry-wide trouble, none for changes in law or accounting rules, and no "only if hit harder than peers" test. This is close to the exact wording a court used to let a buyer cancel the real Akorn / Fresenius merger. Every other contract here is far better protected — this is the deal a reviewer should open first.
